learn.b: One API over four kernel interfaces. How the backend is picked, and what each one changes.

NUCLEI_BACKEND, when set and not empty: auto, io_uring, or the platform’s poller by name (epoll, kqueue, iocp). Else the runtime’s own Builder::backend, if it named one. Else the backend of NucleiConfig, the process’s choice for every runtime that names none. Else auto: io_uring when the kernel lets this process make the ring its shards use, the platform’s poller otherwise. A backend named in any of these ways that the process cannot have fails with the reason when the first shard starts; it never falls back. Proactor::backend() says which one the calling thread’s shard runs. use nuclei::{Builder, IoBackend, Proactor}; fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // What the process picked: NUCLEI_BACKEND if set, else io_uring where it may, else the poller. println!("default: {:?}", Proactor::backend()); // One runtime on the platform's poller, whatever the default is. let poller = if cfg!(target_os = "linux") { IoBackend::Epoll } else if cfg!(windows) { IoBackend::Iocp } else { IoBackend::Kqueue }; let runtime = Builder::new().worker_threads(1).backend(poller).build()?; let used = runtime.block_on(runtime.spawn(async { Proactor::backend() })); assert_eq!(used, poller); Ok(()) }

Linux (and Android) 6.1 or later, with the iouring feature (on by default). The ring is Nuclei’s own, on libc alone. The probe is safe even under a seccomp filter that kills a process for calling io_uring_setup; where io_uring is refused (an older kernel, a container’s policy), auto runs epoll. Each shard owns one ring, enabled and used by the shard’s own thread alone: single issuer with deferred task work, unless a kernel submission thread is configured (sqpoll_wake_interval), which rules those two out. A stream keeps one multishot receive armed, and accept_multi one multishot accept, from the shard’s receive group (configured with recv_buffers and recv_buffer_size). Regular files are read and written with ring operations at the handle’s cursor.

Linux, Android and illumos. On Linux it is what auto picks where io_uring cannot be had, and what NUCLEI_BACKEND=epoll asks for. A readiness poller: the shard’s driver makes each call when the descriptor may be ready, into the shard’s buffers. Your code sees the same completion-style API. Regular files run as pread and pwrite jobs on the blocking pool. A child’s exit comes through its pidfd.
macOS, iOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD and DragonFly. A readiness poller, served like epoll; a child’s exit comes through EVFILT_PROC, wakes through EVFILT_USER. Regular files run on the blocking pool.

Windows. One completion port per shard; operations are overlapped calls the kernel completes. A handle takes std’s TcpStream, TcpListener, UdpSocket and File, and a child’s pipes. There are no Unix sockets on Windows. A pipe or console opened for synchronous IO cannot complete on a port, so its calls run as jobs of the blocking pool and come back to the shard like the kernel’s completions. A TCP write, once issued, is always finished: a cancelled send there may have handed bytes to the stack while saying it took none. Timed waits use a high-resolution waitable timer where the system offers one, so timers are not rounded to the 15.6 ms system tick; elsewhere a wait is rounded up, never ending early.
CI runs the test suite on io_uring and on epoll on Linux 6.1, 6.6 and 6.12, on kqueue on macOS, and on completion ports on Windows, and runs it under AddressSanitizer on both Linux backends.
The messages you may meet, what each one means, and what to change. Each message is quoted as Nuclei prints it.

learn.t: A spawned task never ran, or stopped halfway
learn.b: No message at all: the Task was dropped, and dropping a task cancels it. A loop that spawns per connection and throws the handle away cancels every connection at once. Fix: call .detach() on tasks nobody waits for, or keep the handles and await them. See Tasks.

the task has no output: it was cancelled or its runtime shut down before it completed, or it was awaited again after completing Awaiting a Task whose runtime was dropped or shut down before the task completed panics with this message. Fix: keep the runtime alive until its tasks are done, or await task.fallible(), which gives None in these cases instead of panicking.

learn.t: names no backend of this platform
learn.b: the default runtime could not start: NUCLEI_BACKEND=kqueue names no backend of this platform (use auto, epoll or io_uring) NUCLEI_BACKEND holds a name this system has no backend for. The message lists the names that work here. Fix: set one of the names listed, or unset the variable.

the default runtime could not start: NUCLEI_BACKEND=io_uring asks for io_uring, but this build has no io_uring; leave it unset to use the poller io_uring was asked for by name (through NUCLEI_BACKEND, Builder::backend or NucleiConfig) and this process cannot have it. The reason follows but: here the crate was built without the iouring feature; on another machine it may be the kernel or a sandbox refusing the ring. A backend named by hand never falls back. Fix: leave the backend unset, so auto picks io_uring where it can and the poller where it cannot; or turn the iouring feature back on; or run where io_uring is allowed (Linux 6.1 or later, and a sandbox that permits it).

the proactor is configured already: call `with_config` once, before any IO Proactor::with_config was called twice, or after the first IO, spawn or block_on, which configures the defaults. Fix: call it once, first thing in main. With #[nuclei::main] the body already runs on the runtime, so use a plain fn main that configures and then calls nuclei::block_on, as in Production.

learn.t: the default runtime is already running
learn.b: the default runtime is already running Builder::build_global returned this error: a free function, the attribute or an earlier build_global started the default runtime first. Fix: call build_global before anything spawns, or build a Runtime of your own and use its methods.

block_on is nested 2 deep on one thread, the most allowed: each level runs on the thread's stack (raise the limit with `Builder::max_nesting`) (Here the limit was set to 2; the default is 256.) Each nested block_on runs on the thread’s stack, and one level past the limit panics before the stack would overflow. Fix: await instead of nesting where you can; raise Builder::max_nesting where you cannot.

No message: a task called block_on on a future that waits for that very task. The task is not polled again until the call returns, so neither can finish. Fix: wait for the other work with .await inside the task, not with block_on.

learn.t: Data seems lost, or an error came late
learn.b: Writes are accepted into the stream’s write-behind and sent by the driver, so a failed write can surface on a later write or on flush. Fix: flush().await (or close().await) where you need to know the bytes reached the kernel. See Proactive IO.

learn.t: A child’s wait fails with ECHILD
learn.b: Something other than Nuclei reaped the child: the program ignores SIGCHLD, or calls waitpid itself. Fix: leave SIGCHLD at its default and let Child::wait reap your children.
Handle<T> takes one of std’s own IO types and gives it async operations. TCP, UDP, Unix sockets and files, one section each.

A Handle<T> owns a std IO object (a TcpListener, a UdpSocket, a File) and the source its shard’s driver reaches. The object stays std’s own type: Deref and get_ref hand it out for its own methods (addresses, socket options), and the handle’s async methods and trait impls do the IO. Handle::new(object) takes an object you made yourself, of any type that implements IoObject: on unix anything with a file descriptor, on Windows std’s sockets and files and a child’s pipes. The constructors below make one for you. Handle Async methods Traits Handle<TcpListener> bind, accept, incoming, accept_multi Handle<TcpStream> connect, send, recv, peek, read_owned, write_owned AsyncRead, AsyncWrite, also on &Handle Handle<UdpSocket> bind, connect, send, recv, peek, send_to, recv_from, peek_from Handle<UnixListener> bind, accept, incoming Handle<UnixStream> connect, pair, send, recv, peek, read_owned, write_owned AsyncRead, AsyncWrite, also on &Handle Handle<UnixDatagram> bind, pair, send, recv, peek, send_to, recv_from, peek_from Handle<File> open, read_owned, write_owned AsyncRead, AsyncWrite (also on &Handle), AsyncBufRead, AsyncSeek bind, pair and new are plain functions; everything that waits for the network is async. The Unix types are on Unix only. On Windows a handle takes std’s TcpStream, TcpListener, UdpSocket and File, and a child process’s pipes.

bind makes a listener; port 0 asks the system for a free one. accept gives a connected Handle<TcpStream> and the peer’s address; connect dials out. send and recv move bytes; recv returning Ok(0) means the peer closed its side. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // Port 0 asks the system for a free port; local_addr says which. let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; nuclei::spawn(async move { loop { let Ok((stream, peer)) = listener.accept().await else { break }; println!("accepted {peer}"); nuclei::spawn(async move { let mut buf = [0u8; 1024]; while let Ok(n @ 1..) = stream.recv(&mut buf).await { if stream.send(&buf[..n]).await.is_err() { break; } } }) .detach(); } }) .detach(); let client = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; client.send(b"ping").await?; let mut reply = [0u8; 4]; let n = client.recv(&mut reply).await?; assert_eq!(&reply[..n], b"ping"); Ok(()) }

Streams implement AsyncRead and AsyncWrite, on the handle and on a shared reference to it, so one task can read and write the same stream, and any code written against those traits works with it: buffered readers, line splitting, copy. incoming() is a Stream of accepted connections. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use futures::io::{self, AsyncBufReadExt, AsyncWriteExt, BufReader}; use futures::StreamExt; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; // An echo server in one line: both halves of the copy are the same stream, // since AsyncRead and AsyncWrite are implemented on &Handle<TcpStream> too. nuclei::spawn(async move { let mut incoming = listener.incoming(); while let Some(Ok(stream)) = incoming.next().await { nuclei::spawn(async move { io::copy(&stream, &mut &stream).await }).detach(); } }) .detach(); let mut stream = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; stream.write_all(b"first line\nsecond line\n").await?; stream.flush().await?; let mut lines = BufReader::new(&stream).lines(); assert_eq!(lines.next().await.transpose()?.as_deref(), Some("first line")); assert_eq!(lines.next().await.transpose()?.as_deref(), Some("second line")); Ok(()) }

write_vectored and read_vectored work on every backend, on TCP streams, Unix streams and files (and on a shared reference to each). A vectored write gathers its slices, in order, into the handle’s write-behind in one call: all of them when the write-behind starts empty, as many bytes as fit otherwise. The driver then writes them out like any other write, so the same code behaves the same on io_uring, epoll, kqueue and I/O completion ports. A vectored read scatters the bytes that came in across your slices, in order. A child process’s pipes take the traits’ default instead, which reads into or writes only the first slice that is not empty. use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions}; use std::io::{IoSlice, IoSliceMut}; use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use futures::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // Gather: three slices go into the stream's write-behind together, in one call. let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; let reader = nuclei::spawn(async move { let (mut stream, _) = listener.accept().await?; let mut line = Vec::new(); stream.read_to_end(&mut line).await?; std::io::Result::Ok(line) }); let mut stream = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; let parts = [IoSlice::new(b"GET "), IoSlice::new(b"/ "), IoSlice::new(b"HTTP/1.1")]; assert_eq!(stream.write_vectored(&parts).await?, 14); stream.close().await?; assert_eq!(reader.await?, b"GET / HTTP/1.1"); // Scatter: one read fills the slices in order. let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("learn-nuclei-vectored-{}", std::process::id())); let std_file = OpenOptions::new().write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(&path)?; let mut file = Handle::<File>::new(std_file)?; file.write_vectored(&[IoSlice::new(b"head"), IoSlice::new(b"body!!")]).await?; file.flush().await?; let mut file = Handle::<File>::open(&path).await?; let (mut head, mut body) = ([0u8; 4], [0u8; 6]); let n = file.read_vectored(&mut [IoSliceMut::new(&mut head), IoSliceMut::new(&mut body)]).await?; assert_eq!((n, &head, &body), (10, b"head", b"body!!")); std::fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) }

accept_multi returns a TcpStreamGenerator, a stream of connections that owns its own copy of the listener, so it may outlive the handle. A connection reset before it was taken is skipped; any other error ends the stream, and take_error says what it was. On io_uring it keeps one accept armed for every connection that comes. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use futures::StreamExt; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; // A stream of connections with its own copy of the listener. On io_uring // it keeps one accept armed for every connection that comes. let mut connections = listener.accept_multi().await?; let server = nuclei::spawn(async move { let mut served = 0; while let Some(stream) = connections.next().await { stream.send(b"hi").await.ok(); served += 1; if served == 3 { break; } } // Why the stream ended, if it ended on an error. assert!(connections.take_error().is_none()); served }); for _ in 0..3 { let client = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 2]; client.recv(&mut buf).await?; } assert_eq!(server.await, 3); Ok(()) }

An unconnected socket sends with send_to and receives with recv_from, which also gives the sender’s address. connect fixes a peer; then send and recv talk to it alone. The peek forms read without taking the datagram. use std::net::UdpSocket; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let a = Handle::<UdpSocket>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let b = Handle::<UdpSocket>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; // Datagrams to an address, and from whoever sent them. a.send_to(b"hello", b.local_addr()?).await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 64]; let (n, from) = b.recv_from(&mut buf).await?; assert_eq!((&buf[..n], from), (&b"hello"[..], a.local_addr()?)); // A connected socket sends to and receives from its one peer. let c = Handle::<UdpSocket>::connect(a.local_addr()?).await?; c.send(b"connected").await?; let (n, _) = a.peek_from(&mut buf).await?; assert_eq!(&buf[..n], b"connected"); let n = a.recv(&mut buf).await?; assert_eq!(&buf[..n], b"connected"); Ok(()) }

Unix only. A listener binds a path and accepts streams; pair makes two connected ends with no path at all. A UnixDatagram keeps message boundaries, like UDP. use std::os::unix::net::{UnixDatagram, UnixListener, UnixStream}; use futures::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("learn-nuclei-{}.sock", std::process::id())); let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&path); let listener = Handle::<UnixListener>::bind(&path)?; let server = nuclei::spawn(async move { let (mut stream, _addr) = listener.accept().await?; let mut word = String::new(); stream.read_to_string(&mut word).await?; std::io::Result::Ok(word) }); let mut client = Handle::<UnixStream>::connect(&path).await?; client.write_all(b"over a path").await?; client.close().await?; assert_eq!(server.await?, "over a path"); std::fs::remove_file(&path)?; // A connected pair, no path needed. let (left, right) = Handle::<UnixStream>::pair()?; left.send(b"pair").await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 4]; right.recv(&mut buf).await?; assert_eq!(&buf, b"pair"); // Datagrams keep their boundaries. let (d1, d2) = Handle::<UnixDatagram>::pair()?; d1.send(b"one").await?; d1.send(b"two").await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 8]; assert_eq!(d2.recv(&mut buf).await?, 3); assert_eq!(d2.recv(&mut buf).await?, 3); Ok(()) }

Handle::<File>::open(path).await opens a file for reading, as File::open does. For any other mode, open it with std’s OpenOptions and pass the file to Handle::new. Reads and writes share the handle’s cursor; seek moves it. use std::fs::{File, OpenOptions}; use std::io::SeekFrom; use futures::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncSeekExt, AsyncWriteExt}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("learn-nuclei-{}.txt", std::process::id())); // Open with std's options, then hand the file over. let std_file = OpenOptions::new().read(true).write(true).create(true).truncate(true).open(&path)?; let mut file = Handle::<File>::new(std_file)?; file.write_all(b"one
two
three
").await?; file.flush().await?; file.seek(SeekFrom::Start(4)).await?; let mut rest = String::new(); file.read_to_string(&mut rest).await?; assert_eq!(rest, "two
three
"); // Handle::<File>::open opens for reading. let reader = Handle::<File>::open(&path).await?; // read_owned lends the buffer: the bytes land in it with no copy. let (n, buf) = reader.read_owned(Vec::with_capacity(4)).await; assert_eq!(&buf[..n?], b"one
"); std::fs::remove_file(&path)?; Ok(()) } A regular file is always ready as far as a poller can tell, so on io_uring its reads and writes are ring operations at the cursor, and on the other backends they run as pread and pwrite jobs on the blocking pool; either way no shard waits. A File that is not a regular file (a FIFO, a terminal, a pipe) is a byte stream the driver serves like a socket.

Through Deref every method of the std type works on the handle: local_addr, set_nodelay, set_ttl and the rest. get_mut, DerefMut and into_inner give mutable access or the object itself; before the object can change, the handle delivers the bytes it wrote behind, stops its other pending work and ends its registration, so the driver never touches a descriptor the handle no longer owns; the next operation registers the object again. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; // std's own method, through Deref let stream = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; stream.set_nodelay(true)?; // a socket option, on std's type println!("{} -> {}", stream.local_addr()?, stream.get_ref().peer_addr()?); // Take the std object back out; the handle lets go of it first. let std_stream: TcpStream = stream.into_inner(); std_stream.set_nonblocking(false)?; Ok(()) }

From the first line in Cargo.toml to a server in production. Each chapter takes one idea, explains it, and shows it in a program you can run. Nuclei: proactive async runtime for Rust. A task hands its IO to the driver and gets the result back completed, and every core runs a shard of its own: its tasks, its timers, its buffers and its driver. These chapters teach it from the ground up and cover every way of using it that the crate offers. Every example runs Each program on these pages was compiled and run on Linux, on io_uring and on epoll, before it was published. The ones that need Unix (Unix sockets, Unix signals, Unix programs such as sort) say so.

New to async runtimes: read the chapters in order. Setup, Runtime and Tasks are the core; Proactive IO explains what makes Nuclei different. Moving from a readiness-based runtime: start with Migrate, then read Tasks and Proactive IO. The two behaviours that differ most are what dropping a task handle does and when a write is done. Looking for one function: the API reference is on docs.rs.
Most of what you write today has a direct counterpart. The table maps the usual patterns; the pitfalls below are the places where the same-looking code behaves differently.

An attribute on an async test #[nuclei::test] threads = N gives the test its own runtime. Drop the handle to let the task run on .detach() Dropping a Task cancels it. Abort a task Drop the Task, or task.cancel().await cancel gives back the output if it was already done. The single most common bug after a move. A spawned task whose Task is dropped stops at its next await, and never runs if it had not started. Every fire-and-forget spawn needs .detach(). use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::time::sleep; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // Dropping a Task cancels it: this one never prints. let cancelled = nuclei::spawn(async { sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await; println!("never printed"); }); drop(cancelled); // detach lets a task run to its end without a handle. nuclei::spawn(async { println!("detached, and it still runs"); }) .detach(); // cancel stops a task and gives back its output if it had finished. let slow = nuclei::spawn(async { sleep(Duration::from_secs(10)).await; 1 }); assert_eq!(slow.cancel().await, None); // fallible gives None instead of a panic when the task ended without an output. let done = nuclei::spawn(async { 7 }).fallible(); assert_eq!(done.await, Some(7)); sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await; }

learn.t: A write is accepted, not delivered
learn.b: A write returns once its bytes are copied into the stream’s write-behind. Code that wrote and then exited, or wrote and then dropped the stream while expecting an error right away, should flush().await (or close().await). Bytes written behind are still delivered after a drop, for up to 60 seconds.

A task stays on its shard. A task that computes for a long time without an await holds every other task of that shard, and no idle core takes them over. Move such work to spawn_blocking, or break it up with awaits.

learn.t: Buffers are copied, unless you lend them
learn.b: recv and read copy from the shard’s buffer into your slice; writes copy into the write-behind. Where the copy matters, read_owned and write_owned hand the driver your Vec<u8> and give it back. See Proactive IO.
Proactor::with_config runs once, before the first IO, spawn or block_on; it panics otherwise. Configure from a plain fn main, then enter the runtime with block_on.

The blocking_ forms of the sync types run a nested block_on when called on a Nuclei shard, so the shard keeps running its other tasks. That is safe, but an .await is still the better call inside async code.
Nuclei completes IO for the task that asked. What that means, backend by backend, and what it changes in the code you write.

A reactor tells a task when a socket is ready, and the task then makes the read or write call itself. If another reader got there first, or the readiness was spurious, the call would block, and the task waits again. Nuclei is a proactor. A task hands its operation to its shard’s driver, and the operation completes for that task. No task waits for readiness and then makes the call itself. Every call on a descriptor is the driver’s, made into memory the runtime owns. Backend How an operation completes io_uring The driver submits it to the shard’s ring and the kernel performs it. I/O completion ports It is issued as an overlapped call; the kernel completes it and the shard takes the completion from its port. epoll, kqueue The driver makes the call: at once when the socket may be ready, otherwise on its next edge. The task’s side is the same on all four: it asks, and later takes the result.

The kernel may hold an operation’s memory long after the task that asked has moved on, so Nuclei never lends the kernel memory a future borrows. Instead: A read lands in a buffer of the shard’s pool, and recv (or read) copies it into the slice you passed. A write is copied into the stream’s write-behind buffer and accepted at once; the driver writes it out as the socket takes it, in the order it was written. Owned buffers: read_owned and write_owned take a Vec<u8> and give it back with the result, so the kernel reads into it or writes from it with no copy. Each worker’s pool is bounded by Builder::io_buffer_cap (64 MiB by default). At the cap, IO waits for buffers to come back, so a worker’s IO memory never grows past it.

read_owned reads into the spare capacity of the vector, after the bytes it holds, and gives it back with how many bytes came (zero at the end of the stream, or when the vector has no spare capacity). write_owned writes all of the vector and ends once the kernel took the last byte. Both exist on Handle<TcpStream>, Handle<UnixStream> and Handle<File>. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; let server = nuclei::spawn(async move { let (stream, _) = listener.accept().await?; // Lend the driver this buffer: the kernel reads straight into it, // and the buffer comes back with the result. let buf = Vec::with_capacity(64); let (n, buf) = stream.read_owned(buf).await; let n = n?; // Lend it again for the reply; it comes back once the kernel took every byte. let (sent, _buf) = stream.write_owned(buf[..n].to_vec()).await; sent }); let client = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; let (sent, _) = client.write_owned(b"lent, not copied".to_vec()).await; sent?; let (n, reply) = client.read_owned(Vec::with_capacity(64)).await; assert_eq!(&reply[..n?], b"lent, not copied"); server.await?; Ok(()) }

Because a write is accepted into the write-behind, a successful write means the bytes are Nuclei’s to deliver, not that the kernel has them. flush waits until the kernel took every byte and reports a write that failed; close flushes and then shuts the write side, so the peer sees the end of the stream. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use futures::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt}; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; let reader = nuclei::spawn(async move { let (mut stream, _) = listener.accept().await?; let mut all = Vec::new(); stream.read_to_end(&mut all).await?; std::io::Result::Ok(all.len()) }); let mut stream = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; // Each write is copied into the stream's write-behind and accepted at once; // the driver writes it out as the socket takes it. for _ in 0..1000 { stream.write_all(&[b'x'; 1024]).await?; } // flush waits until the kernel took every byte, and reports a failed write. stream.flush().await?; // close flushes, then shuts the stream's write side, so the reader sees the end. stream.close().await?; assert_eq!(reader.await?, 1000 * 1024); Ok(()) } A write that fails keeps its error: every later write fails with it until a flush reports it. Bytes written behind are delivered whatever happens to the handle, as std’s are: get_mut and into_inner wait until the kernel took them, and a handle dropped before that leaves them to a copy of its descriptor, which delivers them for at most 60 seconds and then closes.

Async code drops futures all the time: a timeout fires, a cancellation token trips, a select takes another future first. Nuclei keeps the bytes safe when that happens: A read whose future is dropped leaves what the driver already read for the next read, so nothing the kernel handed over is lost. A lent read (read_owned) whose future is dropped hands the bytes read into its buffer to the next read, ahead of anything read after them. A lent write (write_owned) whose future is dropped reaches the stream whole or not at all: withdrawn if none of it went out, finished by the driver if some did. On Windows a TCP write is always finished.

On io_uring a stream keeps one multishot receive armed for every arrival: the kernel fills a buffer of the shard’s receive group as bytes come in, so a receive that waits holds no buffer of its own. A listener’s accept_multi works the same way for connections. The receive group’s size is set with recv_buffers and recv_buffer_size in the io_uring configuration (Production); a receive that runs past its share is paused until its reader catches up.
Child processes whose exits and pipes are async, and signals as streams.

nuclei::process::Command describes a process as std::process::Command does (arg, args, env, envs, env_remove, env_clear, current_dir, stdin, stdout, stderr), and as_std and as_std_mut reach the std command for anything it does not mirror. Three ways to run it: output().await: pipes stdout and stderr (and gives the child an empty stdin unless you set one), collects both, and waits for the exit. status().await: waits for the exit; the streams are inherited unless set. spawn(): starts the child and returns a Child at once. This example and the next run Unix programs (echo, true, sort). use nuclei::process::Command; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // Runs the program, collects its stdout and stderr, and waits for its exit. let out = Command::new("echo").arg("hello from a child").output().await?; assert!(out.status.success()); assert_eq!(String::from_utf8_lossy(&out.stdout).trim(), "hello from a child"); // Only the exit status, with the streams inherited. let status = Command::new("true").status().await?; assert_eq!(status.code(), Some(0)); Ok(()) }

A spawned child’s piped streams are async: ChildStdin implements AsyncWrite, and ChildStdout and ChildStderr implement AsyncRead. Take them out of the Child with take(). Drop stdin (or close it) to end the child’s input. use futures::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt}; use nuclei::process::{Command, Stdio}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let mut child = Command::new("sort") .stdin(Stdio::piped()) .stdout(Stdio::piped()) .spawn()?; println!("sort runs as process {}", child.id()); let mut stdin = child.stdin.take().expect("stdin is piped"); stdin.write_all(b"pear
apple
fig
").await?; drop(stdin); // closing stdin lets sort see the end of its input let mut sorted = String::new(); child.stdout.take().expect("stdout is piped").read_to_string(&mut sorted).await?; let status = child.wait().await?; assert!(status.success()); assert_eq!(sorted, "apple
fig
pear
"); Ok(()) } wait().await waits for the exit without holding a thread; a piped stdin is closed first, so a child that reads it to the end can exit. wait_with_output().await also collects the piped stdout and stderr. try_wait() gives the status if the child has exited, without waiting. kill() ends the child: SIGKILL on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows. A shard’s driver reports the exit and reaps the child: through a pidfd on epoll, EVFILT_PROC on kqueue, a wait on the process handle on Windows, and ring operations on io_uring. A wait fails with ECHILD if something else reaped the child first, for example when the program ignores SIGCHLD or calls waitpid itself.

nuclei::signal::ctrl_c().await completes when the process gets a Ctrl-C: SIGINT on Unix, the console’s CTRL_C_EVENT on Windows. Listening starts with the first poll, and from then on the default action of SIGINT (ending the process) is replaced for good. #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { println!("running; press Ctrl-C to stop"); nuclei::signal::ctrl_c().await?; println!("stopping cleanly"); Ok(()) }

nuclei::signal::unix::signal(kind) listens to one signal and returns a Signal, a stream whose every item stands for one delivery or more since the item before; recv().await takes the next. SignalKind names the usual ones (hangup, interrupt, terminate, quit, user_defined1, user_defined2, child, alarm, pipe, window_change) and SignalKind::from_raw takes any number (as_raw gives it back). poll_recv(cx) is the wait of recv for a hand-written poll. use nuclei::signal::unix::{signal, SignalKind}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let mut hangups = signal(SignalKind::hangup())?; let mut terms = signal(SignalKind::terminate())?; println!("process {}: SIGHUP reloads, SIGTERM stops", std::process::id()); nuclei::spawn(async move { // Each item stands for one delivery or more since the last one. while hangups.recv().await.is_some() { println!("reloading"); } }) .detach(); terms.recv().await; println!("stopping"); Ok(()) } signal fails for a number that is no signal, for SIGKILL and SIGSTOP (no handler can take them), and for SIGILL, SIGFPE and SIGSEGV (a handler for them cannot return).

On Windows, nuclei::signal::windows has ctrl_c, ctrl_break, ctrl_close, ctrl_logoff and ctrl_shutdown, each returning a CtrlEvent stream with recv. An event with a listener alive is taken; for close, logoff and shutdown the system ends the process once the handlers return, whatever they say.
Every setting of a runtime, the io_uring configuration, the counters to watch, a clean shutdown, and tests.

Every setting is optional; an unset one takes a default that needs no configuration to work well. use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::{Builder, IoBackend}; fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let backend = if cfg!(target_os = "linux") { IoBackend::Epoll } else { nuclei::Proactor::backend() }; let runtime = Builder::new() .worker_threads(4) // default: one per core .max_worker_threads(8) // default: four times worker_threads .pin_workers(true) // Linux; default true .thread_name_fn(|| "edge".to_string()) // or .thread_name("edge") .thread_stack_size(2 * 1024 * 1024) // default 8 MiB .max_nesting(64) // default 256 .max_blocking_threads(128) // default 512 .thread_keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(5)) // default 10 seconds .local_spawn_margin(16) // default 32 .io_buffer_cap(32 * 1024 * 1024) // default 64 MiB per worker .backend(backend) // default: the process's choice .build()?; let backend_used = runtime.block_on(runtime.spawn(async { nuclei::Proactor::backend() })); println!("workers run {backend_used:?}"); runtime.shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(1)); Ok(()) } Builder method Default What it sets worker_threads(n) one per core Worker threads, each running one shard. Zero runs every task on the thread that spawns it, while that thread is inside block_on. max_worker_threads(n) four times worker_threads The most workers the runtime may start over its life; what spawn_more_threads may add up to. pin_workers(bool) true Whether each worker is pinned to its own core (Linux). A pinned shard keeps its cache warm. thread_name(name), thread_name_fn(f) nuclei-worker, nuclei-blocking The name of every thread the runtime starts. thread_stack_size(bytes) 8 MiB The stack of every thread the runtime starts. max_nesting(depth) 256 How deep block_on may nest on one thread. max_blocking_threads(n) 512 The most threads the blocking pool runs at once. thread_keep_alive(duration) 10 seconds How long an idle blocking thread waits for work before it exits. local_spawn_margin(n) 32 How many more live tasks than another shard a spawning thread’s shard may hold and still take a task it spawns. Zero balances strictly. io_buffer_cap(bytes) 64 MiB The most bytes each worker’s IO buffers hold; at the cap, IO waits for buffers to come back. backend(IoBackend) the process’s choice The kernel interface this runtime’s workers use. One the process cannot have makes build fail with the reason. A non-empty NUCLEI_BACKEND overrides it. build() starts the runtime; build_global() starts it as the process default (see Runtime).

The io_uring ring of every shard is configured once per process, before any IO, with Proactor::with_config. A second call, or a call after IO has started (which configures the defaults), panics. use nuclei::config::{IoUringConfiguration, NucleiConfig}; use nuclei::Proactor; fn main() { // Once, before any IO: the io_uring ring's settings for every shard. Proactor::with_config(NucleiConfig { iouring: IoUringConfiguration { queue_len: 4096, recv_buffers: 512, recv_buffer_size: 16 * 1024, ..IoUringConfiguration::default() }, backend: None, // io_uring where this process may have it, else the poller }); nuclei::block_on(async { println!("IO runs on {:?}", Proactor::backend()); }); } IoUringConfiguration field Default What it sets queue_len 2048 Entries in the submission and completion queues. recv_buffers 256 Buffers in each shard’s group for multishot receives: a power of two up to 32768. Zero turns multishot receives off; each read then takes a buffer of the shard’s own pool. recv_buffer_size 16384 The size of each of those buffers, in bytes. For UDP, make it hold the largest datagram you expect. sqpoll_wake_interval None With Some(ms), a kernel thread polls the submission queue and sleeps after that many idle milliseconds. More CPU, fewer system calls. iopoll_enabled false Busy-waits for completions instead of interrupts. Only for files opened with O_DIRECT on file systems that support polling. per_numa_bounded_worker_count Some(256) The kernel’s limit on io_uring worker threads per NUMA node for IO bound in time (regular files, block devices). per_numa_unbounded_worker_count Some(512) The same limit for IO that may never complete, such as sockets. aggressive_poll false Kept for code written against earlier versions; the ring does not read it. Four presets fill the struct from a queue length: interrupt_driven (no polling; the one to pick when unsure), low_latency_driven and kernel_poll_only (both with a kernel submission thread that sleeps after 2 idle milliseconds), and io_poll (with iopoll_enabled). NucleiConfig also carries backend, the backend of every runtime that names none.

nuclei::stats() takes a snapshot of every shard alive in the process (the workers of each runtime, then the shard of each thread that runs block_on) and of the blocking pools. It reads the shards without stopping them, so a running shard pays nothing for it. Most counts are published by a shard as it is about to wait for work, and by a busy shard at least once every few hundred task runs. #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { nuclei::spawn(async {}).await; let stats = nuclei::stats(); for shard in &stats.shards { println!( "{:?} on {:?}: {} tasks, {} polls, {} IO in flight, {} of {} buffer bytes", shard.worker, shard.backend, shard.tasks, shard.polls, shard.ops_in_flight, shard.buffer_bytes, shard.buffer_cap, ); for (kind, count) in shard.errors.iter() { println!(" {count} errors of kind {kind:?}"); } } println!("{} blocking threads", stats.blocking_threads); } ShardStats field What it counts worker, backend The shard’s place among its runtime’s workers (None for a block_on thread’s shard) and its kernel interface. tasks, polls, remote_wakes Tasks on the shard not done yet; task polls run; tasks woken or spawned onto it from other threads. ops_in_flight, cq_overflows Operations handed to the kernel and not ended (io_uring, IOCP; always 0 on epoll and kqueue); times the kernel held completions for want of room in the completion queue (none is lost). buffer_bytes, buffer_cap, buffer_exhausted Bytes the buffer pool holds; the most it may hold; times IO waited because every byte under the cap was in use. timers, errors Timers armed; IO errors by io::ErrorKind (get, iter), with refused registrations (refused_registrations) and accepts that found no descriptor left (accepts_out_of_descriptors) counted apart. Stats also has blocking_threads and off_shard_errors, the errors of IO run on threads that run no shard.

A server stops taking connections when asked, lets the open ones finish, and gives up after a deadline. A CancellationToken carries the request to every task, ctrl_c raises it, and timeout bounds the drain. use std::net::TcpListener; use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::sync::CancellationToken; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let shutdown = CancellationToken::new(); // Ctrl-C cancels the token. let trigger = shutdown.clone(); nuclei::spawn(async move { if nuclei::signal::ctrl_c().await.is_ok() { trigger.cancel(); } }) .detach(); let mut connections = Vec::new(); println!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?); while let Some(accepted) = shutdown.run_until_cancelled(listener.accept()).await { let (stream, _) = accepted?; let token = shutdown.child_token(); connections.push(nuclei::spawn(async move { let mut buf = [0u8; 1024]; while let Some(Ok(n @ 1..)) = token.run_until_cancelled(stream.recv(&mut buf)).await { let _ = stream.send(&buf[..n]).await; } })); } // Give open connections a moment to finish, then stop. let drain = async { for connection in connections { connection.await; } }; if nuclei::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), drain).await.is_err() { eprintln!("some connections did not finish in time"); } Ok(()) }

learn.t: The process default, the earlier way
learn.b: Programs written against earlier versions of Nuclei set up the default runtime with init or init_with_config; both still work, on the shards. GlobalExecutorConfig sets the workers to start (with_min_threads, or from an environment variable with with_env_var), the most it may run (with_max_threads) and their names (with_thread_name_fn). spawn_more_threads and stop_thread grow and shrink it within those bounds. use nuclei::GlobalExecutorConfig; fn main() { // The default runtime, set up the way earlier versions of nuclei did it. nuclei::init_with_config( GlobalExecutorConfig::default() .with_env_var("APP_WORKERS") // read the worker count from here first .with_min_threads(2) .with_max_threads(4), ); nuclei::block_on(async { let started = nuclei::spawn_more_threads(2).await.expect("workers start"); println!("started {started} more workers"); let stopped = nuclei::stop_thread().await; println!("stopped one: {stopped}"); }); } Code that drove the proactor by hand still can. Proactor::get() is the process’s proactor and config its configuration; wait(max_event_size, duration) drives the calling thread’s shard once: its ready tasks, then its IO (for up to duration, or with None until some comes or wake is called), then the tasks that IO woke. wake ends every wait in progress.

#[nuclei::test] makes an async test: its body runs in block_on on the default runtime, or on a runtime of its own with threads = N. A test may return a Result, like any test. use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream}; use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::Handle; #[nuclei::test] async fn echoes_a_line() -> std::io::Result<()> { let listener = Handle::<TcpListener>::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?; let addr = listener.local_addr()?; nuclei::spawn(async move { let (stream, _) = listener.accept().await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 64]; let n = stream.recv(&mut buf).await?; stream.send(&buf[..n]).await?; std::io::Result::Ok(()) }) .detach(); let client = Handle::<TcpStream>::connect(addr).await?; client.send(b"ping").await?; let mut buf = [0u8; 4]; client.recv(&mut buf).await?; assert_eq!(&buf, b"ping"); Ok(()) } // Its own runtime with one worker, for a test that needs a known shape. #[nuclei::test(threads = 1)] async fn times_out() { let never = std::future::pending::<()>(); assert!(nuclei::time::timeout(Duration::from_millis(10), never).await.is_err()); } cargo test #[nuclei::bench] makes an async benchmark for the nightly test harness: the crate that uses it writes #![feature(test)] and extern crate test; at its root, and each run of the body is timed on block_on.
Where async code starts: the attribute, a plain block_on, a runtime you build yourself, and handles that reach it from anywhere.

#[nuclei::main] turns an async main into a program: its body runs in block_on on the default runtime. It may return anything main may, such as std::io::Result<()>. With threads = N the program builds a runtime of its own with N worker threads instead; threads = 0 runs every task on the thread inside block_on, with no worker at all. #[nuclei::main(threads = 2)] async fn main() { let workers = nuclei::stats().shards.iter().filter(|s| s.worker.is_some()).count(); assert_eq!(workers, 2); println!("{workers} worker shards"); }

nuclei::block_on runs a future to its end on the calling thread, running other tasks of that thread’s shard meanwhile. The first call (or the first spawn) starts the default runtime, so a plain fn main needs nothing else. use std::time::Duration; fn main() { // The first call starts the default runtime: one worker shard per core. let sum = nuclei::block_on(async { nuclei::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)).await; (1..=10).sum::<u32>() }); assert_eq!(sum, 55); } nuclei::drive does the same as block_on; it keeps the name earlier versions used.

block_on works anywhere, inside a task too. On a worker the call nests: the worker’s shard keeps running its other tasks, timers and IO until the future completes. That lets synchronous code deep in a call stack wait on a future without holding the shard up. #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let task = nuclei::spawn(async { // A synchronous helper deep in a call stack can still wait on a future: // block_on nests, and the shard keeps running its other tasks meanwhile. let inner = nuclei::spawn(async { 21 }); nuclei::block_on(inner) * 2 }); assert_eq!(task.await, 42); } Two rules come with it. The task that called block_on is not polled again until the call returns, so a future that waits for that very task never completes. And each level runs on the thread’s stack, so the depth is bounded: 256 levels by default, set with Builder::max_nesting; one more panics with a message that says so.

Runtime::new() starts one with every setting at its default; Runtime::builder() (the same as Builder::new()) sets them. A runtime spawns, runs block_on and runs blocking work, like the free functions do on the default runtime. use std::time::Duration; fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let runtime = nuclei::Runtime::builder() .worker_threads(4) .thread_name("api-worker") .max_blocking_threads(64) .build()?; let task = runtime.spawn(async { "served" }); let out = runtime.block_on(task); println!("{out}"); // Stop the workers, waiting for them at most one second. runtime.shutdown_timeout(Duration::from_secs(1)); Ok(()) } Dropping a Runtime stops its workers, drops the tasks they still hold and waits for the threads to exit. shutdown_timeout bounds that wait: workers still running a task when it passes are left to exit on their own. Production lists every setting.

runtime.handle() gives a RuntimeHandle: cheap to clone, and usable from any thread to spawn on that runtime or to block_on. A handle does not keep its runtime running. fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let runtime = nuclei::Runtime::new()?; let handle = runtime.handle(); // A plain thread hands work to the runtime through its handle. let worker = std::thread::spawn(move || handle.block_on(handle.spawn(async { 2 + 2 }))); assert_eq!(worker.join().unwrap(), 4); Ok(()) }

The free functions (spawn, block_on, spawn_blocking, spawn_local) use the runtime the calling thread is inside, or else the default runtime. To configure the default one, build it with Builder::build_global before anything starts it. RuntimeHandle::current() gives a handle to whichever runtime the thread is inside, or the default one, started on the spot if it is not running. fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // Configure the default runtime before anything starts it. let handle = nuclei::Builder::new().worker_threads(2).build_global()?; // From here on the free functions use it. let task = nuclei::spawn(async { "on the default runtime" }); println!("{}", nuclei::block_on(task)); // A handle to whatever runtime this thread is inside, or the default one. let _same = nuclei::RuntimeHandle::current(); drop(handle); Ok(()) } build_global fails with the default runtime is already running once a free function, the attribute or an earlier build_global has started it. Call it first thing in main.
Add Nuclei to a project, choose its features, run a first program and see which kernel interface it picked.

Rust @@RUST_VERSION@@ or later. Nuclei itself is written in the 2024 edition; your crate may use any edition. It builds for these systems, each on its own kernel interface: System Backend Linux, Android io_uring where the kernel (6.1 or later) and the sandbox allow it, else epoll illumos epoll macOS, iOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFly kqueue Windows I/O completion ports Any other target stops the build with Target OS is not supported.

cargo add nuclei or in Cargo.toml: [dependencies] nuclei = "@@NUCLEI_MINOR@@" Nuclei implements the futures-io traits (AsyncRead, AsyncWrite, AsyncBufRead, AsyncSeek) and the Stream trait of futures-core. The methods you call through them, such as read_to_end, write_all or a stream’s next, come from extension traits. The examples here take those from the futures crate: cargo add futures

#[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let answer = nuclei::spawn(async { 6 * 7 }).await; println!("the answer is {answer}"); } cargo run the answer is 42 #[nuclei::main] runs the async main on the runtime, and nuclei::spawn places a task on one of its shards; awaiting the task gives its output. There is nothing to set up: the first spawn or block_on starts the default runtime, with one worker shard per core the process may run on.

Feature Default What it gives iouring on The io_uring driver, on Linux and Android. Without it those systems run on epoll. epoll on Names epoll beside iouring. Epoll is built on Linux either way. attributes on #[nuclei::main], #[nuclei::test] and #[nuclei::bench], from the nuclei-macros crate. recycle off Node memory for the lock-free queues, maps and channels the runtime is built on, from a per-thread cache over a slab layer instead of the global allocator. recycle is for applications. Cargo turns a feature on for every user of a crate in the build, so a library that enabled it would enable it for all of them. [dependencies] # Without the io_uring driver (Linux runs on epoll), keeping the attribute macros: nuclei = { version = "@@NUCLEI_MINOR@@", default-features = false, features = ["attributes"] } [dependencies] # In an application: node memory from a per-thread cache. nuclei = { version = "@@NUCLEI_MINOR@@", features = ["recycle"] }

fn main() { nuclei::block_on(async { println!("IO runs on {:?}", nuclei::Proactor::backend()); }); } IO runs on IoUring With nothing set, Nuclei takes io_uring where the kernel lets this process make the ring its shards use, and the platform’s poller otherwise. It probes io_uring safely, even under a seccomp filter that kills a process for calling io_uring_setup. The NUCLEI_BACKEND environment variable picks one by hand: auto, io_uring or epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and the BSDs, iocp on Windows. NUCLEI_BACKEND=epoll cargo run A backend named by hand that the process cannot have is an error with the reason, never a silent fallback. Backends has the details, and Errors the messages.
Locks, semaphores, events, once-cells, cancellation and channels whose waits are futures, usable under any executor, and lock-free maps and queues.

Every wait in nuclei::sync is a future built from futures and wakers alone. A task that waits for a lock yields its shard instead of blocking the thread, and the same types work under any executor. Each primitive also has try_ forms that never wait, and blocking_ forms for plain threads. Called inside a Nuclei task, a blocking_ method runs a nested block_on, so the shard keeps running its other tasks. Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore, Notify, Barrier, OnceCell, SetOnce and the mpsc, oneshot, broadcast and watch channels take the names, signatures, error types and documented behaviour of the established async sync API, so code written against that API compiles against these. Nuclei adds Event, Latch, Lazy, the upgradable read of the RwLock, reentrant locks keyed by an Owner, OnceCell::get_or_init_racy and CancellationToken. Dropping a pending wait withdraws its waiter, and anything handed to it in the meantime is passed on, so no wakeup is lost. (A Barrier wait is the one exception: an arrival that was counted stays counted.) Locks and semaphores let a caller take what is free even while others wait, so a release never waits for a sleeping task to run. Fairness is counted, not timed: a woken waiter that loses its retry MAX_BYPASS times (16) is owed a handoff, nobody gets in ahead of it, and the next release goes straight to it.

use std::sync::Arc; use nuclei::sync::{Mutex, RwLock, RwLockUpgradableReadGuard}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // A lock whose wait is a future: a task that waits for it yields its shard. let hits = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64)); let tasks: Vec<_> = (0..100) .map(|_| { let hits = Arc::clone(&hits); nuclei::spawn(async move { *hits.lock().await += 1 }) }) .collect(); for task in tasks { task.await; } assert_eq!(*hits.lock().await, 100); // Many readers or one writer. let config = RwLock::new(String::from("v1")); { let a = config.read().await; let b = config.read().await; assert_eq!((a.as_str(), b.as_str()), ("v1", "v1")); } *config.write().await = String::from("v2"); // An upgradable read: read first, then write without letting go. let guard = config.upgradable_read().await; if guard.as_str() == "v2" { let mut writer = RwLockUpgradableReadGuard::upgrade(guard).await; writer.push_str(".1"); } assert_eq!(*config.read().await, "v2.1"); } Mutex: lock().await, try_lock, blocking_lock, and lock_owned on an Arc<Mutex> (with try_lock_owned and blocking_lock_owned) for a guard that is 'static. RwLock: read, write and upgradable_read, with owned and try_ forms; with_max_readers caps the readers. ReentrantMutex and ReentrantRwLock: locks a holder may take again, keyed by an Owner token rather than a thread, because a task can move between threads and many tasks can share one. Owner::new() makes a token no other owner has had, and Owner::thread() gives the calling thread’s own (a ThreadOwner), for code on plain threads. Guards: MutexGuard::map narrows a guard to a part of the locked value and try_map does it when the part may be missing; the read and write guards of the RwLock map the same way. RwLockWriteGuard::downgrade turns a write into a read in one step, so no writer gets in between.

use std::sync::Arc; use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::sync::{Barrier, Event, Latch, Notify, Semaphore}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // At most two of these run at once. let slots = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(2)); let jobs: Vec<_> = (0..6) .map(|_| { let slots = Arc::clone(&slots); nuclei::spawn(async move { let _permit = slots.acquire().await.expect("the semaphore is open"); nuclei::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)).await; }) }) .collect(); for job in jobs { job.await; } // Notify wakes a waiter; a notify_one with nobody waiting is kept for the next one. let notify = Arc::new(Notify::new()); notify.notify_one(); notify.notified().await; // An event is set once and stays set. let ready = Arc::new(Event::new()); let waiter = nuclei::spawn({ let ready = Arc::clone(&ready); async move { ready.wait().await } }); ready.set(); waiter.await; // A latch opens when its count reaches zero. let started = Arc::new(Latch::new(3)); for _ in 0..3 { let started = Arc::clone(&started); nuclei::spawn(async move { started.count_down() }).detach(); } started.wait().await; // A barrier releases its waiters in groups of n; one of each group leads. let barrier = Arc::new(Barrier::new(3)); let arrivals: Vec<_> = (0..3) .map(|_| { let barrier = Arc::clone(&barrier); nuclei::spawn(async move { barrier.wait().await.is_leader() }) }) .collect(); let mut leaders = 0; for arrival in arrivals { leaders += usize::from(arrival.await); } assert_eq!(leaders, 1); } Semaphore: acquire and acquire_many give a permit that returns itself when dropped (acquire_owned and acquire_many_owned take an Arc<Semaphore> for one that is 'static), and a permit can split and merge. add_permits adds permits, forget_permits removes free ones for good, available_permits counts the free ones, and close makes every wait fail. A semaphore holds at most Semaphore::MAX_PERMITS. Notify: notified().await waits; notify_one wakes one waiter (or the next one to come), notify_waiters wakes all that wait now, and notify_last wakes the newest waiter instead of the oldest. notified_owned waits through an Arc<Notify>. Event: set once, wait forever after. Latch: opens when count_down brings its count to zero. Both have is_set, which looks without waiting. Barrier: releases its waiters in groups of n; one waiter of each group is the leader.

use nuclei::sync::{Lazy, OnceCell, SetOnce}; static GREETING: Lazy<String> = Lazy::new(|| "built on first use".to_string()); static SETTINGS: OnceCell<u16> = OnceCell::const_new(); #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { assert_eq!(Lazy::force(&GREETING).as_str(), "built on first use"); // The first caller runs the async initializer; everyone else waits for it. let port = SETTINGS.get_or_init(|| async { 8080 }).await; assert_eq!(*port, 8080); // SetOnce: readers wait until a writer sets it. let leader = std::sync::Arc::new(SetOnce::<&str>::new()); let follower = nuclei::spawn({ let leader = std::sync::Arc::clone(&leader); async move { *leader.wait().await } }); leader.set("node-a").expect("set once"); assert_eq!(follower.await, "node-a"); } OnceCell::get_or_init runs an async initializer once while other callers wait for it; get_or_init_racy never waits: callers that race all build with a synchronous initializer, one value is published and the rest are dropped. SetOnce is set once, and readers can wait until it is. Lazy builds its value on first access (Lazy::force). get_or_try_init takes an initializer that may fail: its error is returned, and the next caller runs its own. initialized says whether a cell holds a value. OnceCell::new_with(Some(value)) makes a cell that starts full, and const_new_with(value) does it in a static; SetOnce has the same two.

use nuclei::sync::{broadcast, mpsc, oneshot, watch}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // mpsc: many senders, one receiver; a bounded channel waits for room. let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(8); for id in 0..4 { let tx = tx.clone(); nuclei::spawn(async move { for n in 0..10 { tx.send(id * 100 + n).await.expect("the receiver is alive"); } }) .detach(); } drop(tx); // the channel closes once every sender is gone let mut count = 0; while let Some(_value) = rx.recv().await { count += 1; } assert_eq!(count, 40); // An unbounded channel never waits, so plain code can send too. let (utx, mut urx) = mpsc::unbounded_channel(); utx.send("no await needed").unwrap(); assert_eq!(urx.recv().await, Some("no await needed")); // oneshot: one value, from one sender to one receiver; a reply channel. let (reply_tx, reply_rx) = oneshot::channel(); nuclei::spawn(async move { reply_tx.send(42).ok() }).detach(); assert_eq!(reply_rx.await, Ok(42)); // broadcast: every receiver gets every value. let (btx, mut first) = broadcast::channel(16); let mut second = btx.subscribe(); btx.send("deploy").unwrap(); assert_eq!(first.recv().await, Ok("deploy")); assert_eq!(second.recv().await, Ok("deploy")); // watch: receivers see the latest value. let (wtx, mut wrx) = watch::channel("v1"); wtx.send("v2").unwrap(); wrx.changed().await.unwrap(); assert_eq!(*wrx.borrow_and_update(), "v2"); } Channel Shape Note mpsc::channel(n) many senders, one receiver, at most n queued a send waits for room: backpressure mpsc::unbounded_channel() many senders, one receiver send never waits and is a plain function oneshot::channel() one value, one sender, one receiver the receiver is the future; an error if the sender is dropped broadcast::channel(n) many senders, many receivers keeps the last n values, rounded up to a power of two; a receiver that falls behind gets Lagged watch::channel(init) many senders, many receivers keeps only the latest value; changed waits for one not seen yet A channel closes once every sender is gone: the receiver takes what is left, then gets None (an error, for oneshot, broadcast and watch). What one sender sends comes out in the order it was sent.

learn.t: Reserving room, batches and weak senders
learn.b: A bounded sender can take its slot first and send later: reserve().await gives a Permit whose send cannot fail, reserve_owned moves the sender into an OwnedPermit, and reserve_many takes several slots. try_send and try_reserve never wait, and send_timeout waits at most a given time. recv_many takes what is queued, up to a limit, in one call. downgrade makes a WeakSender, which does not keep the channel open; its upgrade gives a sender back while another one lives. use nuclei::sync::mpsc::{self, error::TrySendError}; use nuclei::sync::watch; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<u32>(2); // reserve waits for room and holds it: a send through the permit cannot fail. let permit = tx.reserve().await.expect("the receiver is alive"); permit.send(1); tx.send(2).await.expect("the receiver is alive"); // try_send never waits: with both slots taken it hands the value back. match tx.try_send(3) { Err(TrySendError::Full(value)) => assert_eq!(value, 3), other => panic!("expected a full channel, got {other:?}"), } // recv_many takes what is queued, up to a limit, in one call. let mut batch = Vec::new(); assert_eq!(rx.recv_many(&mut batch, 8).await, 2); assert_eq!(batch, [1, 2]); // A weak sender does not keep the channel open. let weak = tx.downgrade(); assert!(weak.upgrade().is_some()); drop(tx); assert!(weak.upgrade().is_none()); assert_eq!(rx.recv().await, None); // watch: change the value in place, and wait for one that passes a test. let (version_tx, mut version_rx) = watch::channel(1u32); let bumper = version_tx.clone(); nuclei::spawn(async move { for _ in 0..3 { bumper.send_modify(|version| *version += 1); } }) .detach(); let version = *version_rx.wait_for(|version| *version >= 4).await.expect("a sender is alive"); assert_eq!(version, 4); drop(version_tx); } A watch sender changes the value in place with send_modify, or with send_if_modified when the change may be nothing; send_replace returns the value it replaced, and a receiver’s wait_for waits for a value that passes a test. A broadcast receiver’s resubscribe makes another receiver, which takes the values sent from then on.

A CancellationToken is a cancellation signal shared by many tasks, for a shutdown or for one job among many. A clone is the same token: cancelling one cancels all. A child_token is cancelled with its parent and can be cancelled alone, which never cancels the parent; a tree of tokens stops a whole part of a program at once. Like the rest of nuclei::sync, it needs no runtime. use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::sync::CancellationToken; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let shutdown = CancellationToken::new(); let workers: Vec<_> = (0..3) .map(|id| { let token = shutdown.child_token(); nuclei::spawn(async move { let mut ticks = 0; loop { let tick = nuclei::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)); // run_until_cancelled gives None once the token is cancelled. if token.run_until_cancelled(tick).await.is_none() { break; } ticks += 1; } println!("worker {id} stopped after {ticks} ticks"); }) }) .collect(); nuclei::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(30)).await; shutdown.cancel(); // cancelling a parent cancels every child for worker in workers { worker.await; } } Waiting is a future: cancelled().await completes once the token is cancelled, at once if it already is, and dropping it withdraws the wait and nothing else. A drop guard cancels its token when the guard goes, so a token can follow the life of a scope or a task: use nuclei::sync::CancellationToken; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let token = CancellationToken::new(); // cancelled_owned moves a clone of the token into the future, so it can be spawned. let watcher = nuclei::spawn(token.clone().cancelled_owned()); { // A drop guard cancels its token when it goes: here, at the end of this block. let _guard = token.clone().drop_guard(); assert!(!token.is_cancelled()); } assert!(token.is_cancelled()); watcher.await; // disarm gives the token back, and nothing is cancelled. let job = CancellationToken::new().drop_guard().disarm(); assert!(!job.is_cancelled()); // A child is cancelled with its parent, never the other way round. let step = job.child_token(); step.cancel(); assert!(step.is_cancelled() && !job.is_cancelled()); job.cancel(); job.cancelled().await; // completes at once: the token is cancelled println!("job cancelled: {}", job.is_cancelled()); } Method of CancellationToken What it does fn new() -> CancellationToken A token, not cancelled. Default makes the same. fn cancel(&self) Cancels the token and every token derived from it, and wakes every task waiting on any of them. fn is_cancelled(&self) -> bool Whether the token is cancelled: one atomic load. fn child_token(&self) -> CancellationToken A token cancelled with this one, which can also be cancelled alone. A child of a cancelled token starts cancelled. fn cancelled(&self) -> WaitForCancellationFuture<'_> A future that completes once the token is cancelled, at once if it already is. fn cancelled_owned(self) -> WaitForCancellationFutureOwned The same future, owning the token, so it can be spawned or stored. async fn run_until_cancelled<F: Future>(&self, fut: F) -> Option<F::Output> Runs fut and gives its output, or None if the token is cancelled first (then fut is dropped). When both are ready together, the output wins. async fn run_until_cancelled_owned<F: Future>(self, fut: F) -> Option<F::Output> The same, owning the token. fn drop_guard(self) -> DropGuard A guard that cancels the token when it is dropped. disarm gives the token back and cancels nothing; token borrows it. fn drop_guard_ref(&self) -> DropGuardRef<'_> The same guard over a borrowed token. When cancel returns, the token and every descendant that existed when the call began are cancelled and their waiters woken, even where another call got there first. A child created at the same moment is cancelled by the time both calls have returned. The tree costs no memory past the tokens alive: a child leaves its parent’s registry when its last clone goes.

nuclei::sync also holds the lock-free structures of the kovan crates the runtime is built on, so one module has every synchronization structure. None of them waits: they hold state that tasks and threads share, while a channel hands work over. use std::sync::Arc; use nuclei::sync::{ArrayQueue, Atom, HopscotchMap, SegQueue}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // A concurrent map: every method takes &self, and get gives back a clone of the value. let seen = Arc::new(HopscotchMap::new()); let tasks: Vec<_> = (0..4u64) .map(|shard| { let seen = Arc::clone(&seen); nuclei::spawn(async move { for n in 0..100u64 { seen.insert(shard * 1000 + n, n); } }) }) .collect(); for task in tasks { task.await; } assert_eq!(seen.len(), 400); assert_eq!(seen.get(&2042), Some(42)); // compute is one atomic read-modify-write of a key. seen.compute(2042, |value| value.map(|n| n + 1)); assert_eq!(seen.get(&2042), Some(43)); // An unbounded queue for many producers and many consumers. let jobs = SegQueue::new(); jobs.push("parse"); jobs.push("plan"); assert_eq!(jobs.pop(), Some("parse")); // A bounded queue: push hands the value back when it is full. let slots = ArrayQueue::new(1); slots.push(1).expect("there is room"); assert_eq!(slots.push(2), Err(2)); // One value that readers load without a lock while a writer replaces it. let config = Atom::new(String::from("v1")); config.store(String::from("v2")); assert_eq!(*config.load(), "v2"); config.rcu(|old| format!("{old}.1")); assert_eq!(config.load_clone(), "v2.1"); } Type What it is HopscotchMap A concurrent hash map. Every method takes &self: insert, remove, get (a clone of the value), get_or_insert, compute (one atomic read-modify-write of a key), iter and keys. SegQueue An unbounded first-in first-out queue for many producers and many consumers. try_pop tells an empty queue (TryPopError::Empty) from one whose next value is still being written (Busy). ArrayQueue A bounded queue with its capacity fixed by new; push hands the value back when it is full. Atom One value that readers load while a writer replaces it: load, store and swap are wait-free, and rcu applies a change, retrying only when another thread changed the value first.

None of this needs a runtime. Threads that may block use the blocking_ forms: use nuclei::sync::mpsc; fn main() { // The channels need no runtime: plain threads use the blocking forms. let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<u64>(4); let producer = std::thread::spawn(move || { for n in 1..=10 { tx.blocking_send(n).expect("the receiver is alive"); } }); let mut sum = 0; while let Some(n) = rx.blocking_recv() { sum += n; } producer.join().unwrap(); assert_eq!(sum, 55); }
Spawning work, waiting for its result, letting it run on its own or stopping it; tasks that are not Send, and work that blocks.

nuclei::spawn takes a future that is Send + 'static and returns a Task<T>. A task is a future itself: awaiting it gives the task’s output. If the task’s future panics, awaiting the task resumes the panic. #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // Each task is placed on a shard and stays there. let tasks: Vec<_> = (0..8u64) .map(|n| nuclei::spawn(async move { n * n })) .collect(); let mut total = 0; for task in tasks { total += task.await; } assert_eq!(total, 140); }

A task stays on the shard it was placed on: nothing steals it. Spawned on a worker, it stays on that worker unless the worker holds more live tasks than another shard by the runtime’s local_spawn_margin (32 by default). Spawned from any other thread, it goes to that thread’s home shard by the same rule; the first spawn takes the less loaded of two shards picked at random. So a task that waits for what it spawned keeps it on its own thread.

A Task owns its task. Dropping it cancels the task: its future is dropped without being polled again. To let a task run to its end with nobody waiting for it, call detach. use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::time::sleep; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // Dropping a Task cancels it: this one never prints. let cancelled = nuclei::spawn(async { sleep(Duration::from_millis(50)).await; println!("never printed"); }); drop(cancelled); // detach lets a task run to its end without a handle. nuclei::spawn(async { println!("detached, and it still runs"); }) .detach(); // cancel stops a task and gives back its output if it had finished. let slow = nuclei::spawn(async { sleep(Duration::from_secs(10)).await; 1 }); assert_eq!(slow.cancel().await, None); // fallible gives None instead of a panic when the task ended without an output. let done = nuclei::spawn(async { 7 }).fallible(); assert_eq!(done.await, Some(7)); sleep(Duration::from_millis(100)).await; } detach(): the task runs to its end; its output is dropped. cancel().await: cancels the task and waits for its future to be dropped; gives back the output if the task had already completed. fallible(): a handle whose await gives Option<T>, None where awaiting the Task would panic (the task was cancelled, or its runtime shut down before it completed). is_finished(): whether the task completed or was cancelled; awaiting a finished task returns at once. The most common surprise A server loop that spawns a task per connection and drops the handle cancels each connection at once. Write nuclei::spawn(handler).detach(), as every server on these pages does.

nuclei::spawn_local takes a future that need not be Send and keeps it on the calling thread: the worker’s shard inside a task, or the thread’s own shard, where it runs while the thread is inside block_on. use std::cell::RefCell; use std::rc::Rc; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { // Rc is not Send, so this future can only run on the thread that made it. let log = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Vec::new())); let tasks: Vec<_> = (0..3) .map(|n| { let log = Rc::clone(&log); nuclei::spawn_local(async move { log.borrow_mut().push(n) }) }) .collect(); for task in tasks { task.await; } assert_eq!(log.borrow().len(), 3); }

A blocking call (a synchronous file system walk, a CPU-heavy computation, a C library that waits) would hold its shard and every task on it. nuclei::spawn_blocking runs a closure on the runtime’s blocking pool instead and returns a Task for its result. The pool runs at most 512 threads at once by default, and an idle thread exits after 10 seconds; Builder::max_blocking_threads and Builder::thread_keep_alive change both. #[nuclei::main] async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { // Blocking calls go to the blocking pool, so no shard is held up. let listing = nuclei::spawn_blocking(|| std::fs::read_dir(".").map(|dir| dir.count())).await?; println!("{listing} entries here"); let digest = nuclei::spawn_blocking(|| (0..1_000_000u64).fold(0u64, |h, n| h.rotate_left(5) ^ n)).await; println!("digest {digest:x}"); Ok(()) }

A runtime starts its workers when it is built and may start more later, up to Builder::max_worker_threads (four times the workers it started with by default). nuclei::spawn_more_threads(n).await starts up to n more and returns how many started. nuclei::stop_thread() stops one worker, unless only the minimum runs: it takes no new task from then on and exits once its tasks are done; stop_current_thread() stops the worker the calling task runs on. Both return a Task<bool> that says whether a worker was stopped. A stopped worker’s place is not taken again. Production shows them running.
Sleeping, timeouts, deadlines and intervals, each on the timer wheel of the shard that polls it.

nuclei::time measures with std::time::Instant, re-exported as nuclei::time::Instant. Every shard has a timer wheel with millisecond slots: a timer waits at least its duration, rounded up to the next millisecond, and a shard busy with a task fires it once that task yields. Arming and cancelling a timer allocates nothing once the shard’s wheel has grown to the most timers alive at once. Dropping a timer’s future cancels it. The timers work outside Nuclei’s tasks too: a timer polled on another runtime’s thread is fired for it by a shard of the current runtime, or of the default one.

use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::time::{self, Instant}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let start = Instant::now(); time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(20)).await; assert!(start.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(20)); time::sleep_until(Instant::now() + Duration::from_millis(5)).await; // A future that takes too long gives Elapsed. let slow = time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(5)); assert!(time::timeout(Duration::from_millis(10), slow).await.is_err()); // One that is ready in time gives its output. let quick = async { "in time" }; assert_eq!(time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(1), quick).await, Ok("in time")); // The same against a deadline. let deadline = Instant::now() + Duration::from_millis(10); assert!(time::timeout_at(deadline, std::future::pending::<()>()).await.is_err()); } sleep(duration) and sleep_until(instant) return a Sleep. Sleep::reset moves its deadline; deadline and is_elapsed read it. timeout(duration, future) and timeout_at(deadline, future) give Ok(output), or Err(Elapsed) if the time ran out first. The future is polled before the clock is looked at, so one that is ready at once always wins.

interval(period) ticks every period, the first tick at once; interval_at(start, period) starts at start. tick().await gives the instant the tick was due, and poll_tick(cx) is the same wait for a hand-written poll. A period of zero panics. use std::time::Duration; use nuclei::time::{self, MissedTickBehavior}; #[nuclei::main] async fn main() { let mut every = time::interval(Duration::from_millis(10)); // Late ticks are skipped instead of fired in a burst (the default). every.set_missed_tick_behavior(MissedTickBehavior::Skip); let first = every.tick().await; // the first tick is at once for _ in 0..3 { every.tick().await; } assert!(first.elapsed() >= Duration::from_millis(30)); // reset: the next tick is one period from now. every.reset(); every.tick().await; assert_eq!(every.period(), Duration::from_millis(10)); } MissedTickBehavior When the interval was polled late Burst (the default) Every missed tick fires without waiting, one after another, until the interval is back on its schedule. Delay The next tick comes one period after the late one: the schedule moves. Skip Missed ticks are skipped: the next tick is the next one on the original schedule after now.
