Nuclei’s configuration options reside here.
IO_URING Configuration 5.19+ Kernel is required to operate IO_URING.

Standard way to use IO_URING. No polling, purely IRQ awaken IO completion. This is a normal way to process IO, mind that with this approach actual completion time != userland reception of completion. Throughput is low compared to all the other config alternatives.
Low Latency Driven version of IO_URING, where it is suitable for high traffic environments. High throughput low latency solution where it consumes a lot of resources.
Kernel poll only version of IO_URING, where it is suitable for high traffic environments. This version won’t allow aggressive polling on completion queue(CQ).
IOPOLL enabled ring configuration for operating on files with low-latency.
Allowed entries in both submission and completion queues.
SQPOLL kernel thread wake up interval.

Get and/or set the limit for number of io_uring worker threads per NUMA node. per_numa_bounded_worker_count holds the limit for bounded workers, which process I/O operations expected to be bound in time, that is I/O on regular files or block devices. Passing 0 does not change the current limit.

This per_numa_unbounded_worker_count holds the limit for unbounded workers, which carry out I/O operations that can never complete, for instance I/O on sockets. Passing 0 does not change the current limit.

This argument allows aggressively waiting on CQ(completion queue) to have low latency of IO completions. Basically, this argument polls CQEs(completion queue events) directly on cq at userspace. Mind that, using this increase pressure on CPUs from userspace side. With SQPOLL as well, this is a double polling approach, where the kernel takes submissions by itself, processes them and puts completions on the completion queue, which nuclei picks up without latency.

Perform busy-waiting for I/O completion events, as opposed to getting notifications via an asynchronous IRQ (Interrupt Request). This will reduce latency, but increases CPU usage. This is only usable on file systems that support polling and files opened with O_DIRECT.

Buffers in each shard’s pool for multishot receives: the kernel fills one as bytes arrive, so a stream’s receive stays armed for every arrival and a receive that waits holds no buffer of its own. A power of two up to 32768; 0 turns multishot receives off, and each read then takes a buffer of the shard’s own pool for its receive.

The size in bytes of each of those buffers. A receive is stopped once the bytes it handed out and its reader has not taken pass an eighth of the pool (at least one buffer), and asked for again when its reader catches up. What the kernel took for it before the stop stays with it, so a reader with a long backlog may hold more until it reads; other receives take buffers of the shard’s own pool meanwhile.
Nuclei’s proactor configuration.
IO_URING Configuration allows you to configure io_uring backend.

The kernel interface every runtime that names none runs its IO on (Builder::backend names one for one runtime). None (the default) picks io_uring where the kernel lets this process have it and the platform’s poller otherwise; a backend named here that this process cannot have makes the first shard fail with the reason. A non-empty NUCLEI_BACKEND overrides it.
Which kernel interface nuclei’s IO runs on.
kqueue (macOS and the BSDs).
epoll (Linux).
io_uring (Linux).
I/O completion ports (Windows).
Runs future to its end on the calling thread, driving its shard’s IO meanwhile: block_on.
Starts the process default runtime now, with every setting at its default, unless it is running already.
Starts the process default runtime now, as config says, unless it is running already (then config is not used).
Starts up to count more workers on the runtime this thread is inside (or the default one), within its maximum; returns how many started.
Stops the worker this task runs on, as stop_thread stops one: false on a thread that is not a worker of its runtime, or when only the minimum runs.

Stops one worker of the runtime this thread is inside (or the default one), unless only the runtime’s minimum runs: it takes no new task from now on and exits once the tasks it has are done. The task completes with whether a worker was stopped, once it takes no new task.
Copies everything reader gives into writer, then flushes it; answers the bytes copied.

Copies a into b and b into a at once, in the calling task, each direction through a buffer of 8 KiB; a direction whose reader ends closes its writer. Answers the bytes copied each way, (a to b, b to a), once both ended; the first error ends both.
copy_bidirectional with a buffer of a_to_b bytes for one direction and of b_to_a bytes for the other.

Proactive, not reactive A reactor tells a task when a socket is ready, and the task makes the call itself. Nuclei is a proactor: the task hands the operation over, and the result comes back to it. Nuclei, a proactor hand over, take back task driver kernel read: hand it over submit, with the buffer the task’s shard runs other tasks the kernel fills the buffer done: bytes in the buffer the result, to the task One hand-over, one completion. The task never calls the kernel and never retries. On epoll and kqueue the driver makes the call when the socket may be ready; the task’s side stays the same. A reactor wait, wake, call, retry task reactor kernel watch this socket readable wake the task read(): the task makes the call itself would block? back to 2, and wait again the bytes, copied into the task’s buffer A readiness wait, a wake, then the task’s own call, which can find nothing and go back to waiting (dashed: when another reader got there first, or the readiness was spurious). The same read in both. The pictures count steps, not the time they take. Completed by the kernel On io_uring and I/O completion ports the kernel performs the read or the write, in memory the runtime keeps alive until the kernel is done with it. The same contract on epoll and kqueue There the shard’s driver makes the call: at once when the socket may be ready, otherwise on its next edge. The task only ever takes the result. The decisions underneath io_uring first On Linux the runtime tries io_uring and falls back to epoll where the kernel, before 6.1, or a sandbox refuses it. The probe is safe even under a seccomp filter that kills a process for calling io_uring_setup. NUCLEI_BACKEND picks one by hand. Thread per core A shard per worker thread runs its tasks and owns its driver, and on Linux each worker is pinned to its own core. A task stays on the shard it was placed on; nothing steals it. Multishot receives On io_uring one receive stays armed for every arrival: the kernel fills a buffer of the shard’s pool as bytes come in, so a receive that waits holds no buffer of its own. Nested block_on block_on works anywhere, inside a task too, and keeps its shard’s other tasks and IO going while it waits. Descriptors you can trust A handle owns its descriptor. A registration ends before the descriptor closes, and kernel tokens carry a generation, so a reused descriptor number never receives another source’s events. IO memory with a ceiling Each worker’s IO buffers hold at most 64 MiB unless you set otherwise. At the cap, IO waits for buffers to come back, so a worker’s IO memory never grows past it. Cancel-safe IO Dropping a future halfway loses nothing. A read cut off by a timeout leaves the bytes the driver already took for the next read, and a lent buffer reaches the stream whole or not at all. Vectored on every backend write_vectored gathers its slices into the write-behind in one call, all of them when it starts empty, on io_uring, epoll, kqueue and IOCP alike; read_vectored scatters what came in across yours. Streams and files both. Workers that grow and drain A running runtime starts more workers, up to its maximum, with spawn_more_threads, and drains them with stop_thread: a stopped worker takes no new task and exits once its tasks are done. Fairness counted, not timed Locks and semaphores let a caller take what is free even while others wait, so a release never waits for a sleeping task. A waiter passed over 16 times is owed a handoff: nobody gets in ahead of it, and the next release goes straight to it.
